blocks.text: The two major contemporary classificatory systems are **ICD-10** (1992) and **DSM-IV** (1994). The American Psychiatric Association produces **DSM**; **World Health Organization** commissioned **ICD-10**.

**DSM-5** was released in 2013 but has been much criticised and, as of the notes, had not been adopted widely except by clinicians communicating with insurers in the **United States**. **ICD-11** was anticipated to be released in 2017 (outdated: see 'ICD-11 date (resolved)' below).

Both **ICD-10** and **DSM-IV** are categorical systems based on clinical descriptions. They are diagnostic and classificatory systems meant to provide reliable diagnosis, but they do not provide assessment plans, case formulations or treatment plans.
Four properties of classificatory systems are flagged as important for Paper A: operationalised criteria, atheoretical approach, hierarchical organisation and multi-axial classification.

Operationalised approach: first introduced in **DSM-III**. Operational criteria use precise clinical descriptions of disorders, predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and details of the number and duration of symptoms required. It enables algorithm-based diagnosis using intensity, duration of symptoms and impairment tests - roughly a checklist, although some rules are necessary and some optional.

Inclusion and exclusion criteria with an explicit number and duration of symptoms = the **OPERATIONALISED** approach. The explanation defines it as clear clinical descriptions plus explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria and the number and duration of symptoms required; the other options offered (atheoretical, multiaxial, aetiological, descriptive) are **NOT** what supplies those criteria.

blocks.text: Inclusion and exclusion criteria: operationalised systems often give a hierarchy of symptoms in order of importance (criterion A, B etc.), which form the core inclusion/exclusion criteria. Computerised scoring systems such as **Operational Criteria Checklist for Psychotic Illness** (for **ICD-10**) facilitate applying operationalised diagnoses.

Atheoretical approach: diseases are described by observed phenomenology, not by understanding of what might cause the disturbance. Aetiological schools such as behaviourism or psychoanalysis are not employed; only neutral observations are taken into account.

Both **ICD** and **DSM** are **ATHEORETICAL**, so '**ICD-10** is theoretical' and '**DSM-IV** is theoretical' are the wrong options. Most diagnoses rest on a few core symptoms plus some ancillary symptoms, and not every listed symptom can be reliably diagnosed (loss of libido more reliably than anhedonia); theoretical assumptions such as psychodynamic theory do not make a classification reliable.

Descriptive approach: classifies illness by what constitutes it rather than what causes it. Lack of pathogenetic knowledge of most psychiatric disorders makes this approach more rational, and it forms the basis of any atheoretical classification.

Current systems entertain categorical diagnoses only (like medical diseases): a presentation either meets or does not meet the criteria for a disorder, as a patient has or does not have pneumonia. Contrast this with blood pressure, measured on a continuum and only categorical once labelled 'hypertension'. The need for a dimensional system is said to be more urgent for personality disorders.

rows: Doctors are accustomed to thinking in categories, so easy to understand; but poor validity - vague categories such as 'Psychosis - not specified' are needed to include atypical cases
More valid, as most emotional and cognitive states exist as a continuum with no clear cut-off between ill and well
All existing knowledge on presentation, aetiology, epidemiology, course, prognosis and treatment is based on these categories
Categories are easy to communicate to professionals
Severity can be better indicated; the need to entertain many comorbid diagnoses may be prevented
Studies using dimensional scales as end points have much greater power to detect group differences than studies of dichotomous categories
Questionable, as dimensions cannot be directly mapped onto clinical decisions such as starting or stopping an intervention

blocks.text: Hierarchical organisation is largely abandoned in **DSM** and somewhat maintained in **ICD-10** in its organisation of chapters. Hierarchy means certain disorders take precedence over others; it follows Jasperian ideas - the ladder runs from organic disorders through substance use, psychosis, affective and neurosis, up to personality issues.

If a disorder higher in the hierarchy can explain the observed symptoms, a diagnosis from lower down should not be entertained even if the symptoms suggest it. Examples: schizophrenic symptoms in Huntington's disease, temporal lobe epilepsy or severe learning disability do not change the diagnosis to schizophrenia; in co-occurring depression and agoraphobia, depression and **obsessive-compulsive disorder**, or organic delirium and psychosis, the first diagnosis is primarily entertained.

The hierarchy is generally non-reflexive: each disorder tends to manifest the symptoms of those lower down but not those higher up. Comorbidity can still be entertained and is explicitly encouraged when using **DSM** (e.g. alcohol use disorder comorbid with depressive disorder).

A working diagnosis of depressive relapse in a woman with a past depressive episode who now fears panic attacks outside the home is keyed to the **HIERARCHICAL** principle - not the atheoretical, descriptive, multiaxial or operationalised principle. The explanation adds that the ideal system would label diseases by aetiology, but as aetiology is mostly unknown, classification groups diseases by common clinical features, shared natural history and treatment response within a hierarchy.

Operationalised approach (DSM-III onward): precise descriptions, inclusion/exclusion criteria, number and duration of symptoms; checklist-like, algorithm-based diagnosis.

Characteristic = common to many disorders; discriminating (e.g. thought insertion) = needed because absent elsewhere; pathognomonic (e.g. flashbacks in post-traumatic stress disorder) = strongly favour one diagnosis.
Atheoretical/descriptive: classify by observed phenomenology, not aetiology (no behaviourist or psychoanalytic schools).

Hierarchy (Jaspers): organic - substance use - psychosis - affective/neurosis - personality; higher disorder explaining symptoms excludes lower diagnosis. Largely abandoned in DSM; comorbidity encouraged.

Multi-axial: ICD-10 has 3 axes (disorder; disability; psychosocial problems); DSM-IV has 5 axes (I clinical, II personality/mental retardation, III medical, IV psychosocial, V Global Assessment of Functioning).

blocks.text: **ICD-10** history: the first **ICD** (1855) was a nomenclature of causes of death. **World Health Organization** adopted it in 1948 after many revisions, calling it **ISCD** 6 (Sixth Revision of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases, Injuries and Causes of Death).
**ICD-10** is a general medical classification intended for worldwide, multi-specialty use, tested in more than 51 countries and found generally applicable.
**ICD-10** has 21 chapters. Roman numeral V and the letter F mark mental and behavioural disorders as the fifth chapter. Codes use an open alpha-numeric system Fxx.xx from **F00** to **F99**.

blocks.text: **DSM-5** has three sections: (1) an introduction and guidance to use; (2) an outline of the diagnostic categories with newly revised chapters; (3) conditions requiring further research before being considered formal disorders, plus details on cultural formulations.

**DSM-5** modified the multiaxial system that separately identified personality disorders (Axis **II**) and medical conditions (Axis **III**): the source notes (p6) print that it now includes only three axes - psychiatric disorder, associated psychosocial and environmental factors, and severity of associated disability - so personality disorders are treated with the same importance as other psychiatric disorders, moving **DSM**'s multiaxial system closer to **ICD**'s. Corrected reading: **DSM-5** has moved to a nonaxial system, with separate notations for psychosocial factors (formerly Axis **IV**) and disability (formerly Axis V), as stated in the explanation to **Question 48** (see 'Axes in DSM-5 (resolved)' in section 1A); expect exam answers to follow the nonaxial position. **DSM-IV** Axis 4 = psychosocial and environmental factors contributing to a psychiatric disorder - not the psychiatric disorder itself, general medical health, personality traits or intellectual ability. The explanation adds that **DSM-5** has abolished the multiaxial system.

blocks.text: **ICD-10** duration criteria: **ICD-10** rejects the assumption that schizophrenia is necessarily long-lasting. Acute psychotic episodes are diagnosed for up to one month; if schizophrenic features are continuous the diagnosis is reclassified as schizophrenia after a month. If not, an acute psychotic episode diagnosis is valid for up to 3 months, after which other diagnoses such as persistent delusional disorder may be entertained. Prodromal symptoms are not included in the 1-month criterion.

**ICD-10** is the **MORE** **LENIENT** system for schizophrenia: one month of symptoms is enough, whereas **DSM-IV** requires six months - so 'requires 6 months criteria for schizophrenia' is the option that is **NOT** a feature of **ICD-10** in this **EXCEPT** question (the other options **ICD-10** does have: schizotypal disorders under schizophrenia, acute polymorphic psychosis, post-psychotic depression under schizophrenia, dissocial personality disorder).

sections.title: 4B. Classification of psychosis: other psychotic disorders

blocks.text: Acute and transient psychotic disorders (**ICD-10**): onset within two weeks is described as acute and onset within 48 hours as abrupt. Complete recovery within 2 to 3 months is the rule. The form may be polymorphic or schizophrenia-like; in acute polymorphic psychosis, several hallucinations and delusions change in type and intensity from day to day or even within the same day.

Schizotypal disorder is diagnosed in patients with eccentric manners, social withdrawal, magical thinking, suspiciousness and obsessive ruminations without resistance (ruminations may have dysmorphophobic contents). At least a 2-year history, with schizophrenia never diagnosed in the past, is needed. It includes older descriptions such as borderline schizophrenia and pseudoneurotic schizophrenia.

Schizotypal disorder is classified with schizophrenia and related disorders in **ICD-10** but with Cluster A personality disorders in **DSM-IV**. Schizotypy is more common in other first-degree relatives of schizophrenic subjects than in the general population, and relatives of schizotypal subjects have an increased risk of schizophrenia.

Schizotypal is **NOT** an **ICD-10** personality disorder: it is classified with **F20** (schizophrenia) - the odd one out in a 'which is not an **ICD-10** personality disorder' question whose other options are anankastic, paranoid, schizoid and emotionally unstable borderline.

Persistent delusional disorders: a persistent, often life-long, typically 'non-bizarre' delusion or set of related delusions arising insidiously in mid-life or later. Transient auditory hallucinations may occur; clear persistent voices, schizophrenic symptoms such as delusions of control, marked blunting of affect and definite brain disease are incompatible with the diagnosis. Occasional or transitory auditory hallucinations, particularly in elderly patients, do not rule it out.

In persistent delusional disorder the delusions need not be strictly monothematic (though mostly are). Affect, thought and behaviour are globally normal, but patients' attitudes and actions in response to the delusions are appropriate and may lead to dangerousness in some cases.

blocks.text: Induced delusional disorders are a distinct diagnostic category, coded **F24** in **ICD-10**: a rare disorder in which delusions are shared by usually 2 (occasionally more) persons with tightly knit emotional bonds. Only one person has genuine delusions due to underlying psychiatric disorder, most often schizophrenia or delusional disorder. On separation the dependent individual may give up the delusions, and the patient with genuine delusions should be treated appropriately.

Induced delusional disorder is most common between **COUPLES**: most cases occur within the nuclear family, usually between married or common-law couples (==52%==) or sisters (==24%==) - not 'family blood relations' in general, children and adolescents, or groups of men or women.

blocks.text: In induced delusional disorder, induced hallucinations can be present without negating the diagnosis. It is also called symbiotic psychosis or folie a deux; more common in couples and often involves non-bizarre delusions.

Schizoaffective disorder is placed with **F20** (psychoses), not **F30** (affective disorders). Schizophrenic and mood symptoms are seen simultaneously in approximately equal proportion. Mood-incongruent delusions are suggestive but not sufficient: at least one typical schizophrenic symptom must be present (affect-neutral delusions also count as incongruent). Aetiology is assumed intermediate between schizophrenia and affective disorder.

blocks.title: Schizoaffective subtypes
rows: Usually less florid; depressive symptoms more likely to signal a chronic course
Variable; may develop chronic negative symptoms
Respond well to mood stabilisers; recover rapidly

blocks.caption: Shaded box headed DSM-5 AND SCHIZOAFFECTIVE DISORDER, with the two statements printed in it.

blocks.title: DSM-5 and schizoaffective disorder
rows: A major mood episode (not merely mood symptoms) must be present for a majority (not merely 'substantial duration') of the disorder's total duration after Criterion A has been met
Diagnosis takes a more longitudinal perspective compared to **DSM-IV**

blocks.title: Atypical psychotic disorders (recognised but not categorised separately in ICD-10)
rows: Psychosis of sudden onset 'like a bolt from the blue'; polymorphous delusions and hallucinations of any kind; clouded consciousness with emotional instability; absence of physical signs (not caused by an organic mental disorder); rapid return to premorbid functioning; relapses may occur but episodes are separated by symptom-free intervals; arises in a predisposed individual, caused by psychosocial factors, tends to recover and never ends in deterioration

Langfeldt split psychoses diagnosed as schizophrenia into a poor-prognosis 'genuine' or 'process' group and a good-prognosis 'schizophreniform' group; later re-classification of his 100 cases found most 'schizophreniform' psychoses were affective disorders with psychotic features

Endogenous psychotic syndromes with sudden onset, an admixture of affective and schizophrenic symptoms and phasic course; three forms: motility, confusional, anxiety-blissfulness psychoses; predominate in severe postpartum psychiatric disorders and more common in women

Psychotic episodes of sudden onset, mostly unrelated to stress, good immediate outcome but high recurrence risk, with mood swings (depression to elation) and at least two of: perplexity/confusion; delusions (reference, influence, persecution) and/or hallucinations incongruent with mood; motility disturbances (hypo- or hyperkinesia); occasional elation; states of overwhelming anxiety (pananxiety)

blocks.text: **EMI** **ICD-11** diagnostic features: mania = persecutory delusion (common in psychotic mania, next only to grandiose) and affective changes; delirium = transient delusion and visual hallucinations (visual outnumber auditory); delusional disorder = systematised delusion and persecutory delusion (usually single, well systematised, often persecutory, without hallucinations).

bullets.text: ICD-10 acute and transient psychotic disorder: onset within 2 weeks = acute, within 48 hours = abrupt; recovery in 2-3 months is the rule.
Schizotypal disorder: eccentricity, magical thinking, obsessions without resistance; at least 2 years; ICD-10 puts it with schizophrenia, DSM-IV with Cluster A.
Persistent delusional disorder: non-bizarre, mid-life or later onset, functioning preserved; ICD-10 needs 3 months, DSM-IV 1 month.
DSM-5 drops the non-bizarre requirement and abolishes shared delusional disorder as a separate diagnosis.
DSM-IV delusional subtypes: erotomanic, grandiose, jealous (Othello), persecutory (commonest), somatic, mixed/unspecified.
Induced delusional disorder (F24, folie a deux): one genuine patient, dependent partner may drop delusions on separation; common in couples.
Schizoaffective disorder sits under F20 not F30; schizomanic = affective family history, good mood-stabiliser response; schizodepressive = schizophrenia family history, more chronic.
Atypical psychoses: bouffee delirante (Legrain), process schizophrenia (Langfeldt 1939), cycloid psychoses (Leonhard 1957; postpartum, women).
Schizotypal disorder is not an ICD-10 personality disorder; it is classified with F20 (schizophrenia).
Delusional disorder: circumscribed non-bizarre delusions; bizarre delusions are least likely.

sections.title: 5A. Classification of mood disorders: depression and bipolar disorder

blocks.caption: Table: Depressive disorder - DSM-IV Major Depressive Disorder vs ICD 10 Depressive disorder (duration; the nine DSM-IV symptoms; ICD-10 criterion A and criterion B symptoms), with the footnote on weight loss.

blocks.title: Depressive episode: DSM-IV major depressive disorder vs ICD-10 depressive disorder
rows: Most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks
At least two weeks usually required, for depressive episodes of all three grades of severity
At least one symptom must be depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure
Criterion A: depressed mood, loss of interest and enjoyment, and reduced energy leading to increased fatigability and diminished activity

Five or more of nine symptoms in total: depressed mood; loss of interest; significant weight loss or gain, or decrease/increase in appetite; insomnia or hypersomnia; psychomotor agitation or retardation; fatigue or loss of energy; worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; diminished ability to think or concentrate or indecisiveness; recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation without plan, attempt or plan

Criterion B: reduced concentration and attention; reduced self-esteem and self-confidence; ideas of guilt and unworthiness; bleak and pessimistic views of the future; ideas or acts of self-harm or suicide; disturbed sleep; diminished appetite
Weight loss must be unintentional and at least ==5%== of weight in one month to qualify; reduced self-confidence is not listed in **DSM**

blocks.title: ICD-10 '4-6-8' rule for severity grading of depression

blocks.text: **ICD-10** grades depression severity by symptom counts, but **PSYCHOTIC** **FEATURES** override the count: irrespective of the total symptom count, psychotic symptoms contribute towards classifying a depressive episode as severe - the keyed answer over psychomotor retardation, somatic symptoms, suicidal ideas or a history of mania.

Both **DSM** and **ICD-10** define recurrent major depressive disorder when there is more than one episode of depression. In **ICD-10** the diagnosis can be given if there has been at least one previous major depressive episode separated from the current one by at least two months.

blocks.caption: Shaded box headed DSM-5 AND DEPRESSION, with the two statements printed in it.

blocks.title: DSM-5 and depression
rows: In **DSM-IV** a diagnosis of depression could not be given in the presence of bereavement for 2 months after the loss; this exclusion is now removed
A specifier 'with anxious distress' is added to rate severity of bipolar or depressive disorders, taking **DSM** closer to **ICD**'s description of mixed anxiety and depression

blocks.text: Bipolar affective disorder is characterised by periods of prolonged and profound depression alternating with periods of excessively elevated and irritable mood, known as mania. Type 1 is characterised by full-blown mania or mixed mania and depression; type 2 by recurrent depression and hypomania without episodes of mania or mixed states.

**ICD-10** needs at least two mood episodes, with complete recovery in between, before a bipolar diagnosis can be considered. In **DSM**, bipolar disorder can be diagnosed even with a single manic episode.

Except in the elderly, the natural course of mood episodes is that mania lasts about 4 months and depression about 6 months. In the elderly, episodes are considerably longer, with shorter inter-episodic remissions and more frequent episodes.

**ICD-10** bipolar affective disorder subcategories: current episode hypomanic; manic without psychotic symptoms; manic with psychotic symptoms; mild or moderate depression; severe depression without psychotic symptoms; severe depression with psychotic symptoms; mixed; currently in remission; other bipolar affective disorders; unspecified.

blocks.caption: Boxed list headed ICD-10 bipolar affective disorder, giving the current-episode categories (hypomanic; manic without/with psychotic symptoms; mild or moderate depression; severe depression without/with psychotic symptoms; mixed), Currently in remission, and Other bipolar affective disorders: Bipolar affective disorder, unspecified.
Table: DSM IV Manic episode vs ICD 10 Manic episode (duration, criterion A, criterion B / symptom lists).

blocks.title: Manic episode: DSM-IV vs ICD-10
rows: At least 1 week, or any duration if hospitalised
Sustained for at least a week (unless severe enough to require admission)
Abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood
Mood predominantly elevated, expansive or irritable and definitely abnormal for the individual
Three (or more) from the list, four if mood only irritable
At least three, four if mood merely irritable, leading to severe interference with personal functioning

Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep; more talkative or pressure to talk; flight of ideas or racing thoughts; distractibility; increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation; excessive involvement in pleasurable activities with high potential for painful consequences

Increased activity or restlessness; increased talkativeness (pressure of speech); flight of ideas or racing thoughts; loss of normal social inhibitions; decreased need for sleep; inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; distractibility or constant changes in activity or plans; foolhardy or reckless behaviour (spending sprees, reckless driving); marked sexual energy or indiscretions

blocks.text: **DSM-5** mania lists **REDUCED** **NEED** **FOR** **SLEEP**, not insomnia: 'insomnia/hypersomnia' is the option **NOT** included in the manic-episode criteria, while increased energy, flight of ideas, being much more talkative and inflated self-esteem/grandiosity are.

Psychotic symptoms in mania: mood symptoms are prominent but severe mania may have psychotic symptoms (usually mood-congruent, may be incongruent). Delusions and hallucinations are often 'changeable'. Grandiose and persecutory delusions are common; auditory hallucinations are usually second person and consistent with mood (e.g. religious revelations).

Hypomania shares symptoms with mania to a lesser degree: not severe enough to interfere with social or occupational functioning, require admission, or include psychotic features. It includes mildly elevated, expansive or irritable mood, increased energy and activity, increased self-esteem, talkativeness, over-familiarity, reduced need for sleep and difficulty focusing on one task.

Hypomanic episode is the one **NOT** known to carry psychotic features: by definition hypomania is not severe enough to interfere with social or occupational functioning, require hospital admission or include psychotic features. Manic episode, psychotic depression, acute and transient psychotic disorder and schizoaffective disorder are the options where psychotic features occur.

blocks.text: Mixed states: manic/hypomanic and depressive symptoms occur simultaneously in a single episode, present every day for at least 1 week (**DSM-IV**) or 2 weeks (**ICD-10**).

blocks.title: DSM-IV course specifiers for bipolar disorder
rows: At least four episodes within one year; 70-==80%== of rapid cyclers are women; associated with tricyclic antidepressant use, low thyroxine, female sex, bipolar type 2 pattern and neurological disease
Fluctuations over days or even hours
Onset of mania, hypomania or depression within 4 weeks of childbirth
Recurrences over several years with most episodes starting (and ending) at the same time each year

blocks.text: Rapid cycling (four or more mood episodes a year) is **ASSOCIATED** **WITH** **ANTIDEPRESSANT** **USE** - but the explanation says the relationship may be associative rather than causal, because depressive episodes that precede rapid cycling trigger the prescription. Hyperthyroidism, alcohol abuse, menopause and stressful life events are the distractors.

blocks.text: Secondary mania can result from misuse of alcohol or illicit drugs and from prescribed drugs such as **levodopa** and corticosteroids (wanes with drug clearance), and from organic conditions such as thyroid disease, multiple sclerosis and lesions of cortical and/or subcortical brain areas.
Bipolar 3 describes minimal depression complicated by antidepressant-induced hypomania; these patients fall into the bipolar spectrum (coded in **ICD** as unspecified type).

Hypomania precipitated by antidepressants in a patient with dysthymia = 'bipolar **III**' (hypomania or mania precipitated by antidepressant drugs); the explanation warns that **DSM-5** files this as 'substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder' and does not call it 'Bipolar **III** disorder'. Bipolar **II**, double depression, cyclothymia and bipolar I are the distractors.

blocks.text: A first depressive episode on an **SSRI** followed by about 5 days of overactivity, distractibility, irritability and sleeplessness: **SSRI**-induced mood switch is not a recognised **ICD** or **DSM** category, but a hypomanic period plus a depressive history = **BIPOLAR** **II**, not unipolar mania, mixed affective disorder, bipolar I or substance-induced mood disorder.

Separate description of mixed episode removed; new specifier 'with mixed features' added - no need to fulfil full criteria for both mania and major depressive episode simultaneously; some features of the opposite pole are sufficient

bullets.text: Depressive episode needs at least 2 weeks in both systems; DSM-IV needs 5+ of 9 symptoms including depressed mood or loss of interest; ICD-10 has core criterion A (depressed mood, loss of interest/enjoyment, reduced energy) plus criterion B.
ICD-10 4-6-8 rule: at least 2 core symptoms plus 4 total = mild, 6 = moderate, 8 = severe.
Recurrent depression in ICD-10 needs a previous episode separated by at least 2 months; DSM-5 removes the bereavement exclusion and adds 'with anxious distress'.
ICD-10 bipolar needs 2 mood episodes; DSM allows a single manic episode. Minimum durations: depression 2 weeks, mania 7 days, hypomania 4 days, mixed 2 weeks.
Bipolar 1 = mania or mixed; bipolar 2 = recurrent depression with hypomania, no mania or mixed states.
Natural course: mania about 4 months, depression about 6 months (longer in the elderly).
Mania: at least 3 symptoms (4 if only irritable) for at least a week; mixed states 1 week DSM-IV or 2 weeks ICD-10; hypomania has no psychosis and does not impair function.

Rapid cycling = 4+ episodes a year, 70-80% women, linked with tricyclic antidepressant use, low thyroxine, bipolar 2 and neurological disease; DSM-5 replaces mixed episode with a 'with mixed features' specifier.
ICD-10: psychotic features make a depressive episode severe regardless of the symptom count.
DSM-5 mania lists reduced need for sleep, not insomnia/hypersomnia.

sections.title: 5B. Classification of mood disorders: persistent and seasonal affective disorders

blocks.text: Persistent affective disorders include dysthymia and cyclothymia, respectively the unipolar and bipolar patterns of symptoms that fail to meet criteria for severity but are of long duration and sufficient to cause impairment.

Dysthymia (**ICD-10**) / dysthymic disorder (**DSM-IV**): chronic, mildly depressed mood and diminished enjoyment, not severe enough to be a depressive illness. Clinical features include depressed mood (the source prints '< 2yrs'; reviewer correction, not in the source: dysthymia lasts at least 2 years, at least 1 year in children and adolescents in DSM-IV), reduced/increased appetite, insomnia/hypersomnia, reduced energy/fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration and thoughts of hopelessness.
Double depression describes episodes of major depression superimposed on dysthymia; prognosis and treatment response may be worse.

Cyclothymia: a subclinical presentation with oscillating high and low moods (numerous periods of mild depression and mild elation) without ever having a significant manic or depressive episode, and not severe or prolonged enough for bipolar affective disorder or recurrent depressive disorder. The individual usually perceives the mood swings as unrelated to life events.

blocks.title: Seasonal affective disorder in ICD-10 (Annex)
rows: 3 or more affective episodes, onset within the same 90-day period of the year, for 3 or more consecutive years; remissions within a defined 90-day period; seasonal episodes substantially outnumber any non-seasonal episodes
Most commonly depressive, with atypical features: hypersomnia, increased appetite, carbohydrate craving, weight gain
Onset commonly in autumn/winter (less daylight); resolution in spring/summer
The classical seasonal presentation of depression with reversed biological features in winter does not constitute **seasonal affective disorder**

Bright light (10,000 lux) superior to dim light; daily exposure usually 1 to 2 hours; benefit may be apparent within a few days; maintenance treatment for the next few months until the usual time of remission. Reviewer correction (not in the source): the usual regimen is 10,000 lux for about 30 minutes daily (or 2,500 lux for about 2 hours); the source's '10,000 lux for 1 to 2 hours' appears to mix the two regimens.

blocks.text: **DSM-5** and dysthymia: dysthymia of **DSM-IV** is reclassified as persistent depressive disorder, a diagnosis that includes both chronic major depressive disorder and the previous dysthymic disorder.

blocks.caption: Shaded box headed DSM-5 AND DYSTHYMIA, with the statement printed in it.

blocks.text: Cyclothymia frequently fails to come to medical attention: its mood swings are mild and mood elevation may be enjoyable (increased activity, productivity, self-confidence and sociability), so people present because of depressive episodes affecting social/work life or comorbid drug/alcohol misuse, and if drugs are contemplated it is a trial of a mood stabiliser.

bullets.text: Dysthymia (unipolar) and cyclothymia (bipolar) are persistent affective disorders: long-lasting (reviewer correction, not in the source: dysthymia at least 2 years; the notes print '< 2yrs'), mild, but impairing.
Double depression = major depression on top of dysthymia; prognosis and treatment response may be worse.
Cyclothymia: oscillating mild highs and lows, never meeting criteria for bipolar or recurrent depression; often fails to come to medical attention.
ICD-10 seasonal affective disorder: 3+ episodes in the same 90-day period for 3+ consecutive years, seasonal episodes outnumber non-seasonal; autumn/winter onset with atypical features.

Phototherapy for seasonal affective disorder: 10,000 lux, 1-2 hours daily as printed in the notes (reviewer correction, not in the source: 10,000 lux for about 30 minutes, or 2,500 lux for about 2 hours); benefit within days, maintained until the usual remission time.
DSM-5: dysthymia becomes persistent depressive disorder (chronic major depressive disorder plus dysthymic disorder).

facts.value: 1 to 2 hours daily as printed (reviewer correction, not in the source: about 30 minutes at 10,000 lux, or 2 hours at 2,500 lux)

sections.title: 6A. Classification of neurotic disorders: anxiety and phobic disorders

blocks.text: Although the term 'neurotic' is retained, neurosis is not a major organising principle in **ICD-10**; **DSM** abandoned the name completely in 1994. **ICD-10** groups 'Neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders' under seven headings: phobic anxiety disorders; anxiety disorders (including panic disorder and generalised anxiety); obsessive-compulsive disorders; reaction to severe stress and adjustment disorders; dissociative (conversion) disorders; somatoform disorders; other neurotic disorders.

blocks.title: Anxiety-related classification: ICD-10 vs DSM-IV
rows: At least 6 months, symptoms on most days
Not stated in the source notes. Reviewer addition (not in the source): at least 6 months, more days than not, with at least 3 of 6 symptoms

Agoraphobia is the primary diagnosis; panic disorder is a qualifier for subcategorisation (and a diagnosis in its own right only when no phobic disorder is notable); panic attacks indicate severity of agoraphobia
Agoraphobia is not a distinct diagnosis - only diagnosed along with panic disorder; panic primary

blocks.text: Anxiety disorders include various combinations of psychological and physical symptoms not attributable to real danger, occurring as a persisting state (generalised anxiety disorder) or in attacks (panic disorder).

Generalised anxiety disorder is characterised by prominent tension, excessive worry, generalised free-floating persistent anxiety and apprehension about everyday events leading to significant stress and functional impairment.

blocks.title: ICD-10 generalised anxiety disorder: at least 4 symptoms (at least 1 from autonomic arousal) (list adapted from Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry, 2nd edition, p357)
rows: Breathing difficulties; choking sensation; chest pain/discomfort; nausea/abdominal distress
Feeling dizzy, unsteady, faint or lightheaded; derealisation/depersonalisation; fear of losing control, going crazy, passing out, dying
Hot flushes/cold chills; numbness or tingling sensations
Muscle tension/aches and pains; restlessness/inability to relax; feeling keyed up, on edge or mentally tense; a lump in the throat or difficulty swallowing
Exaggerated startle responses; concentration difficulties/mind going blank; persistent irritability; difficulty getting to sleep due to worrying

blocks.text: Panic attack: a discrete episode of intense anxiety that starts abruptly, peaks within a few minutes (10 minutes) and subsides within 20-30 minutes; usually spontaneous with no obvious precipitant. **DSM-IV** specifies 13 physical symptoms of which at least 4 must be present, and three types: situationally bound/cued, situationally predisposed, and unexpected/uncued.

blocks.caption: Shaded box headed DSM-5 AND PANIC DISORDER, with the two statements printed in it.

blocks.title: Panic disorder criteria
rows: Recurrent panic attacks not secondary to substance misuse, medical conditions or another psychiatric disorder; frequency from many a day to a few a year; persistent worry about further attacks, phobic avoidance and behavioural change; symptoms present for at least one month

Several severe panic attacks within about 1 month: (1) in circumstances with no objective danger; (2) not confined to known or predictable situations; (3) comparative freedom from anxiety between attacks (anticipatory anxiety is common)
Severe if more than 4 attacks per week in a 4-week period
At least one attack followed for 1 month or more by at least one of: anticipation of further attacks; worry about implications; avoidance behaviour

Panic disorder and agoraphobia are separated into two distinct diagnoses, each with separate criteria (comorbid diagnosis still possible); only 2 types of panic attack recognised: unexpected and expected

blocks.title: Marks' cardinal features of phobia
rows: Is out of proportion to the situation
Cannot be explained or reasoned away

blocks.text: Phobic anxiety is subjectively and behaviourally indistinguishable from other anxieties; anticipatory anxiety is important. The phobic object is almost always external and not 'currently dangerous'. Internal phobic objects (nosophobia, dysmorphophobia) are classified under hypochondriasis. Triggers include situations (crowded places), objects (cockroaches) and natural phenomena (thunder). Common types: agoraphobia, social phobia and specific (simple) phobias.

blocks.title: Agoraphobia
rows: Commonest phobic disorder seen by psychiatrists; considered the most incapacitating phobia; lifetime prevalence about 6-==10%== (Weismann and Merikangas 1986)
More common in women aged 15-35; most begin in early or mid-twenties with a further peak in the mid-thirties; in later life may develop secondary to physical frailty
Typically waiting for public transport or shopping in a crowded supermarket; lack of an immediately available escape route is the main cognitive basis for the anxiety
Distance from home, crowding and confinement; anticipatory anxiety can start hours before entering the feared situation

Avoidance of crowds, public places, travel away from home or being alone; symptom-free if avoidance successful; symptoms fluctuate; may become totally housebound ('housebound housewife syndrome'); may be accompanied by panic attacks
If depression starts earlier, a depressive disorder diagnosis should suffice, especially in late-onset agoraphobia

blocks.title: Social phobia
rows: Occurs more in small group settings where close scrutiny is possible; blushing and fear of vomiting in public are more common in social phobia
(1) Discrete: anxiety on specific occasions e.g. shy bladder or public speaking; (2) diffuse: with exposure to any generic social task
Usually between ages 17 and 30; first episode in a public place, usually without apparent reason

Marked and persistent fear of social or performance situations with exposure to unfamiliar people or possible scrutiny; fear of humiliating or embarrassing oneself (helps distinguish from anxiety due to paranoia); sufferer must recognise the fear as excessive or unreasonable
Situations involve peer interactions; recognition that the fear is unreasonable not required; 6-month duration specified only for children, not adults

blocks.text: Social phobia vs agoraphobia: both can present as house-bound behaviour and avoidance of public places, but in social phobia the underlying fear is of embarrassing oneself ('doing something stupid') while others are watching - so a fear of being under continuous scrutiny from others points to social phobia, not agoraphobia.

blocks.caption: Shaded box headed DSM-5 AND SPECIFIC PHOBIAS, with the two statements printed in it.

blocks.title: Specific phobias
rows: Mostly childhood: animals average age 7, blood phobia 9, dental phobia 12 (Ost 1987), claustrophobia about 20; more common in women
Animals; aspects of the natural environment; blood/injection/injury; situational; other provoking agents
Does not usually fluctuate and remains constant
Disease phobia related to situations where disease can be acquired and avoided is still a specific phobia, not hypochondriasis
Fainting response with low **blood pressure** and bradycardia rather than tachycardia/sympathetic response; high prevalence among first-degree relatives (Marks 1988)
About ==5%== of adults fear dental procedures, sometimes avoiding all treatment until dangerous caries develop (Gale and Ayer 1969)
Adults (not children) must recognise the fear as unreasonable; 6-month duration only for children
No requirement for adults to recognise the fear as excessive or unreasonable; duration of 6 months or more applies to all ages

blocks.text: **NO** **AVOIDANCE** = **NO** **PHOBIA**: in phobias of all kinds the feared situation is avoided, so a man with a childhood fear of darkness who is not distressed and takes no special measures to avoid dark spaces has **NO** specific phobia - not 'a specific phobia because the fear is irrational' or 'because it began in childhood'.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. A mock explanation: women (less so men) with agoraphobia report significantly more childhood separation anxiety than those with other anxiety disorders, so separation anxiety disorder is keyed as increasing the later risk of panic disorder and agoraphobia.

blocks.subtopic: UNCONFIRMED: ICD-10 panic disorder severity wording
blocks.note: NEEDS VERIFICATION: the notes (and this guide) say ICD-10 panic disorder is severe if more than 4 attacks per week over 4 weeks. sections.title: 6B. Classification of neurotic disorders: obsessive-compulsive disorder, stress reactions, adjustment, grief and post-traumatic stress disorder

blocks.text: **Obsessive-compulsive disorder** is characterised by obsessional thinking, compulsive behaviour and often marked anxiety and depression. **ICD-10**: obsessions (thoughts, images, ideas) and compulsions share these features, all required: (1) acknowledged as originating in the patient's mind; (2) repetitive and unpleasant, at least one recognised as excessive or unreasonable; (3) at least one unsuccessfully resisted (resistance may be minimal in some); (4) carrying out the obsessive thought or compulsive act is not intrinsically pleasurable.

Obsessions can occur as thoughts, ruminations, doubts, impulses and phobias; obsessional slowness can result from obsessional doubts or compulsive rituals. **ICD-10**: obsessions or compulsions (or both) present on most days for at least two successive weeks.

blocks.title: Common obsessive-compulsive disorder symptoms (Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry data)

blocks.text: Compulsive hoarding may be a neurobiologically distinct form of **obsessive-compulsive disorder** and is notoriously difficult to treat by psychological or pharmacological means. Symmetry obsessions tend to be chronic and treatment resistant.

blocks.title: DSM-5 and obsessive-compulsive disorder
rows: New exclusive chapter for obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (no longer clubbed with anxiety disorders); **DSM-IV** described **obsessive-compulsive disorder** as an anxiety disorder along with **generalised anxiety disorder** and **post-traumatic stress disorder**
New diagnosis 1: Hoarding Disorder - core symptom inability (or persistent difficulty) to discard or give up possessions regardless of actual value
New diagnosis 2: Excoriation Disorder (dermatillomania) - core symptom compulsively picking one's own skin for no apparent reason

blocks.text: Acute stress reaction (**ICD**): usually starts within an hour; resolution begins within 8 hours (if the stress is 'hit and run') or 48 hours if the stress is prolonged. Physical exhaustion, organic factors or disease states raise the risk. The stressor poses a serious threat to security, integrity and social position. The patient may be dazed with narrowed attention and disorientation; agitation and overactivity, partial or complete amnesia, and predominance of dissociative symptoms can occur. A history of previous psychiatric disorder does **NOT** negate the diagnosis.

Acute stress disorder is a **DSM** concept similar to acute stress reaction: starts while experiencing or after the event, lasting at least two days to at most four weeks; emphasis on dissociation. **DSM-IV** requires marked anxiety symptoms and 3 of 5 dissociative symptoms (depersonalisation, derealisation, numbing/detachment, reduced awareness of surroundings, dissociative amnesia) and a response of intense fear, helplessness or horror. Debriefing is widely used but with little evidence of effectiveness and may be counterproductive.

Reconceptualised as a heterogeneous array of stress-response syndromes after exposure to a distressing (traumatic or non-traumatic) event
No longer a residual category for other anxiety disorders

blocks.text: Three weeks after a collision with insomnia, poor concentration, nightmares and emotional outbursts = **ACUTE** **STRESS** **DISORDER**: **post-traumatic stress disorder**-like symptoms (intrusion, avoidance, negative mood, hyperarousal) lasting no more than 4 weeks - so post-traumatic stress disorder is the tempting wrong answer at 3 weeks, alongside adjustment disorder, dysthymia and depressive episode.

blocks.text: Adjustment disorder is a diagnosis in both **ICD-10** and **DSM-IV** (in **DSM-IV** a residual category for clinically significant distress not meeting criteria for a more discrete disorder such as depression or **post-traumatic stress disorder**). It refers to psychological reactions in adapting to new circumstances after a non-catastrophic psychosocial stressor such as divorce or separation.

Adjustment disorder presentations: anxiety, depression, poor concentration, irritability, anger, with autonomic symptoms such as tremor and palpitations. Individual vulnerability plays a greater role than in any other neurotic disorder; patients may feel vulnerable to violence though rarely are violent; conduct problems in adolescence and regression in children. Onset is more gradual than acute stress reaction, course more prolonged, social functioning usually impaired.

blocks.title: Adjustment disorder timing
rows: Cannot exceed six months, except the subtype prolonged depressive reaction (up to 2 years)
Lasts only up to a month

blocks.text: Adjustment disorder (depressive reaction) vs major depressive disorder: the symptoms are phenomenologically the **SAME** and both can follow a stressful life event - what distinguishes adjustment disorder is resolution of symptoms within 6 months of the end of the stressor.
Patients bereaved within the last three months cannot be diagnosed with adjustment disorder. Normal bereavement is not coded in **ICD-10** Chapter V but in Chapter **XXI**.

Normal grief: disbelief, shock, numbness, feelings of unreality; anger; guilt; sadness and tearfulness; pining or searching and preoccupation with the deceased; disturbed sleep and appetite, occasionally weight loss; seeing or hearing the deceased ('hallucinations of widowhood'). A typical grief reaction lasts up to 12 months with an average of 6 months.

blocks.caption: Table of grief phases: Phase I Shock and protest, Phase II Preoccupation, Phase III Disorganisation, Phase IV Resolution, each with its printed description.

blocks.text: A third of people who lose a spouse meet criteria for major depression in the first month after the death, and half of these remain depressed a year later. In normal grief substantial improvement is expected within two to six months; those still meeting criteria for major depression after this should receive antidepressant or psychotherapy.

blocks.title: Abnormal (morbid, pathological, complicated) grief (Working with grieving adults, BJPsych Advances)
rows: Grief that is very intense, prolonged, delayed (or absent), or with symptoms outside the normal range: worthlessness, thoughts of self-harm or suicide, excessive guilt, marked slowing of thoughts and movements, prolonged inability to function, hallucinatory experiences (other than the deceased's image or voice)
Absence of expected grief symptoms at any stage
Avoidance of painful symptoms within two weeks of loss
Continued significant grief-related symptoms six months after loss
Sudden unexpected death; insecure survivor; dependent or ambivalent relationship with the deceased; dependent children (cannot show grief easily); previous psychiatric disorder in the survivor

blocks.text: Delusional guilt or intense suicidal ideas nine months after a bereavement point to a major depressive episode rather than bereavement: a widow who still attends her usual social groups but now has pervasive guilt and suicidal thoughts has **DEPRESSION**, not bereavement, paraphrenia, delusional disorder or dementia.

**Post-traumatic stress disorder** is an intense, prolonged and sometimes delayed reaction to an intensely stressful event; essential features are hyperarousal, re-experiencing of aspects of the event and avoidance of reminders.

blocks.title: Principal symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder
rows: Persistent anxiety; irritability; insomnia; poor concentration; hypervigilance and enhanced startle response
Recurrent distressing dreams; intrusive imagery (flashbacks, vivid memories); difficulty recalling stressful events at will

Avoiding thoughts, feelings or conversations about the trauma and activities, places or people that arouse recollections; reviewer correction (not in the source): inability to recall an important aspect of the trauma belongs in this avoidance cluster, whereas the source notes list 'difficulty recalling stressful events at will' under intrusions (retained in that row)
Feeling of detachment or estrangement from others; emotional numbness; diminished interest in activities (anhedonia)

blocks.text: Both **ICD-10** and **DSM-IV** require 2 or more persistent symptoms of increased psychological sensitivity and arousal (not present before the stressor). **Post-traumatic stress disorder** should start within six months of the trauma; in a small number onset is delayed beyond six months ('probable **post-traumatic stress disorder**'), in others the course is chronic (> 6 months). Enduring personality changes are also reported. **DSM-IV** uses a 3-month threshold for chronic **post-traumatic stress disorder**.

bullets.text: ICD-10 obsessive-compulsive disorder: obsessions/compulsions on most days for at least two weeks; acknowledged as own thoughts, resisted, not pleasurable. Commonest symptom checking 63%, washing 50%.
DSM-5: obsessive-compulsive disorder gets its own chapter, with new Hoarding Disorder and Excoriation Disorder; DSM-IV counted obsessive-compulsive disorder as an anxiety disorder.

Acute stress reaction (ICD): starts within an hour, resolves in 8 hours (hit and run) or 48 hours (prolonged); previous psychiatric history does not negate it. Acute stress disorder (DSM): 2 days to 4 weeks, 3 of 5 dissociative symptoms; debriefing is of little proven value.

Adjustment disorder: onset within 1 month (ICD-10) or 3 months (DSM-IV); lasts up to 6 months, prolonged depressive reaction up to 2 years, brief depressive reaction up to 1 month; excluded within 3 months of bereavement.
Normal grief lasts up to 12 months (average 6).
Grief phases: shock and protest, preoccupation, disorganisation, resolution. Abnormal grief: inhibited, delayed, chronic; coded as adjustment disorder in ICD-10.
Post-traumatic stress disorder: hyperarousal, re-experiencing, avoidance; onset within 6 months of the trauma; 2 or more persistent arousal symptoms; chronic if > 6 months (DSM-IV 3 months).
DSM-5 post-traumatic stress disorder: stressor made explicit (direct, witnessed, indirect), subjective fear criterion removed, 4 clusters, children under 6 criterion.
Acute stress disorder = post-traumatic stress disorder-like symptoms lasting no more than 4 weeks.

sections.title: 6C. Classification of neurotic disorders: dissociative, somatoform, other neurotic and factitious disorders

blocks.text: **ICD-10** dissociative (conversion) disorders include dissociative amnesia, fugue, trance/possession and disorders of movement and sensation (motor disorders, convulsions, anaesthesia/sensory loss).

Dissociation is loss of integration among memories, identity, sensations and movements, occurring closely in time with trauma. Theoretical concepts such as unconscious motivation or secondary gain are not used to describe it in **ICD-10**. It starts suddenly and ends abruptly within weeks to months; treatment is difficult if it becomes chronic (nearly a year).

blocks.title: Dissociative amnesia: characteristics
rows: Loss of memory for important recent events, partial, patchy and selective
Episodic memory loss: retrograde only, no anterograde deficits
Events in a discrete period of minutes to years
Not vague or inefficient retrieval but strikingly complete unavailability of memories that were formed and previously accessible; events are traumatic or stressful

blocks.title: Dissociative states described in the notes
rows: Purposeful journey away from home or usual base; self-care usually maintained; a new identity may be assumed with amnesia for past identity during the fugue, and on recovery amnesia for the fugue; no cognitive impairment so behaviour usually normal; perplexity and la belle indifference frequent; amnesia can be part of fugue

Narrowed consciousness with limited but repeated movements; diagnosed only if involuntary, intrusive on life activities and outside culturally sanctioned situations; temporal lobe epilepsy and head injury can cause 'organic' trance

A dissociative disorder of motor movement and sensations; degree of disability very variable; la belle indifference is common but not universal; relatives or friends may have had the organic illness whose symptoms are copied; a milder transient variety in adolescent girls

Adjustment disorder, Munchausen syndrome, hypochondriasis and somatisation disorder are the distractors.

blocks.text: Deliberate self-harm, left-sided somatosensory symptoms, affective disorder and a family history of psychiatric disorder are more often found in non-epileptic than in true epileptic seizures - the **EXCEPTION** in this question is a **STEREOTYPED** pattern of motor symptoms.

**ICD-10** somatoform disorders include somatisation disorder, hypochondriacal disorder, somatoform pain syndromes, autonomic dysfunction and undifferentiated somatoform disorder. All are characterised by lack of a psychological appraisal by the patient and resistance to considering the problem as 'mental' in origin.

Somatisation disorder: (a) at least 2 years of multiple, variable physical symptoms without adequate physical explanation; (b) persistent refusal to accept the reassurance of several doctors; (c) notable impairment of social and family functioning. Also called Briquet syndrome or St Louis hysteria. Family history of alcohol use and antisocial personality is common in women with somatisation disorder.

Nausea, abdominal pain and dysmenorrhoea with no cause found despite investigation = **SOMATISATION** **DISORDER**: physical symptoms involving more than one part of the body with no physical cause, which are real and not created or faked on purpose - the distinction from Munchausen/factitious disorder, hypochondriasis and conversion disorder, the other options.

Hypochondriacal disorder has two conditions: (1) persistent belief of harbouring at least one serious physical illness despite repeated negative investigations, or persistent preoccupation with a presumed deformity (body dysmorphic type); (2) persistent refusal to accept reassurance. Nosophobia and non-delusional dysmorphophobia are classified as hypochondriasis in **ICD-10**. A 6-month duration is specified in the **ICD** diagnostic criteria for research only.

Body dysmorphic disorder (dysmorphophobia) is a separate entity within **DSM-IV** somatoform disorders: an excessive concern (overvalued idea) about trivial or non-existent physical abnormalities. Beliefs of delusional intensity are classified under delusional disorders. Common complaints involve nose, ears, eyes, mouth, buttocks, penis, breasts; patients re-examine, check, groom to hide the defect and avoid. Usually begins in adolescence and is chronic; may occur with depression, schizophrenia, social phobia or personality disorders.
Hypochondriasis affects men and women equally; the patient looks for a diagnosis rather than symptom relief, names the suspected disorder and may be more or less convinced.

Somatoform autonomic syndrome: recurrent autonomic arousal symptoms (palpitations, sweating, tremor, flushing) with subjective symptoms referred to a specific organ or system despite no structural/functional deficit; patients refuse reassurance. Somatoform pain syndrome: persistent, severe, distressing pain not explained by a physiological process or physical disorder. Other somatoform disorders: globus hystericus, psychogenic pruritus, psychogenic torticollis, bruxism, psychogenic dysmenorrhoea.

Sweating, tremor, palpitation and persistent precordial pain for 10 months despite a negative cardiac work-up = **SOMATOFORM** **AUTONOMIC** **DYSFUNCTION**: autonomic arousal symptoms attributed by the patient to a physical disorder of an organ system (cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, respiratory, genitourinary) with no underlying physical disorder - not generalised anxiety disorder, somatisation disorder or conversion disorder.

Diagnoses of somatisation, hypochondriasis, pain disorder and undifferentiated somatoform disorder are eliminated

**Somatic symptom disorder** can be diagnosed even if a medical disorder explains the symptoms; emphasis shifts from physical symptoms to maladaptive thoughts and feelings around them ('positive features')
High health anxiety without somatic symptoms = 'illness anxiety disorder'

blocks.text: Other neurotic disorders include neurasthenia, depersonalisation-derealisation syndrome and other specified neurotic disorders (most culture-bound syndromes such as latah, dhat, koro); psychogenic syncope and writer's cramp are also described here.

Neurasthenia (**ICD-10** **F48**): persistent distressing complaints of increased fatigue after mental effort, or of bodily weakness and exhaustion after minimal effort, with at least two of: muscular aches and pains, dizziness, tension headaches, sleep disturbance, inability to relax, irritability, dyspepsia. Diagnosed only if disorders in **F40-47** or depression cannot account for the symptoms. It is the closest **ICD-10** equivalent of chronic fatigue syndrome.

Depersonalisation-derealisation syndrome: depersonalisation or derealisation present with full insight and a clear sensorium. Depersonalisation = one's feelings/experiences perceived as detached, distant, not one's own, lost; derealisation = objects, people or surroundings seem unreal, distant, artificial, colourless or lifeless. **DSM** classifies it as a dissociative disorder.

Factitious disorders and malingering: **DSM-IV** considered them in a separate chapter. In **ICD-10** factitious disorders are considered with personality disorders (**F68**). Malingering is not an **ICD-10** mental disorder category but coded **Z76**.5. Munchausen by proxy is not coded in Chapter V but discussed in **T74**.8.

Pseudoseizure clues: emotional trigger, gradual onset, closed eyes resisting opening, pelvic thrusting, prolonged episodes, no response to antiepileptics, tongue-tip biting.

Somatisation disorder: 2 years of multiple physical symptoms, refuses reassurance (Briquet/St Louis hysteria); hypochondriasis: belief in a serious illness or deformity; 6-month duration only in ICD-DCR.
DSM-5 replaces somatoform with Somatic Symptom Disorders; illness anxiety disorder for health anxiety without somatic symptoms; BDD moves to obsessive-compulsive disorder chapter.
Neurasthenia (F48) is the closest ICD-10 equivalent of chronic fatigue syndrome; depersonalisation-derealisation requires full insight and clear sensorium.

Hypochondriasis = preoccupied with diagnosis ('one dreadful disease'); somatisation = preoccupied with symptoms ('one excellent cure'); malingering = intentional with external gain; factitious = sick role only.
Sudden aphonia with normal examination = dissociative motor disorder (ICD-10).
A stereotyped pattern of motor symptoms is NOT more typical of non-epileptic seizures.

sections.title: 7A. Disturbances of behaviour and body physiology: eating disorders

blocks.text: **ICD-10** Chapter V (mental health) recognises only non-organic sleep disorders in which emotional causes are a primary factor: dyssomnias (abnormalities in amount, quality or timing of sleep) and parasomnias (abnormal episodic events occurring during sleep).

blocks.text: Sleep walking and sleep terrors are mostly childhood disorders; adult onset or persistence suggests significant psychological disturbance. They are sometimes seen in early dementia, especially **rapid eye movement** disorders in Lewy body dementia. In sleep terrors there are several minutes of disorientation on waking and perhaps perseverative behaviour; recall, if any, is fragmentary. In contrast nightmares are well recalled and may be associated with benzodiazepine, tricyclic or thioridazine use.

Kleine-Levin syndrome: periodic episodes of hypersomnolence and hyperphagia, with poor concentration, mood changes, sometimes hypersexuality and anxiety. **Electroencephalogram** may show nonspecific changes; clinical presentation and tests are normal between episodes. Most often presents in adolescent males, with complete recovery by the 3rd to 4th decade; possible precipitants are excessive workload, febrile illness and respiratory infections.

Kleine-Levin syndrome = periodic episodes of hypersomnolence and hyperphagia, with lack of concentration, mood changes, sometimes hypersexuality and anxiety - **DROP** **ATTACKS** are the option that is **NOT** part of it.

Narcolepsy: excessive daytime drowsiness with sudden onset of **rapid eye movement** sleep (sleep attacks) and sudden loss of muscle tone provoked by strong emotions (cataplexy). Sleep paralysis (inability to move between wakefulness and sleep) and hypnagogic hallucinations (usually auditory, may be visual or tactile; about ==25%== of patients) also occur but less commonly. Attacks usually begin in adolescence and persist for life. Virtually always familial; ==99.5%== of patients have **human leukocyte antigen** antigen **DR-2** (**DR15**/**DQ6**); usually no structural brain lesion.

Excessive daytime sleepiness with auditory hallucinations on waking and episodes of feeling 'pinned down' after waking = **NARCOLEPSY**: hypnopompic hallucinations and sleep paralysis are its characteristic symptoms, so schizophrenia, **rapid eye movement** behavioural disorder, sleep terror and primary hypersomnia are the wrong options.

Sleep terrors: disorientation on waking, fragmentary recall; nightmares: well recalled, linked with benzodiazepines, tricyclics, thioridazine; adult sleepwalking suggests psychological disturbance or early dementia.
Kleine-Levin: periodic hypersomnolence and hyperphagia, adolescent males, recovers by 3rd-4th decade.
Narcolepsy: daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations (25%); familial; 99.5% human leukocyte antigen DR-2 (DR15/DQ6).

International Classification of Sleep Disorders: dyssomnias vs parasomnias (arousal disorders from non-rapid eye movement; transition disorders; rapid eye movement parasomnias such as rapid eye movement behaviour disorder and nightmares).
Sexual dysfunction = F52; DSM-IV groups: desire, arousal, orgasmic, pain.
DSM-5 merges vaginismus and dyspareunia (Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder) and removes sexual aversion disorder.

sections.title: 8B. Disorders of adult personality and behaviour: habit and impulse disorders, gender identity and paraphilias

blocks.text: Impulse control disorders (**DSM-IV**) or habit and impulse disorders (**ICD-10** chapter **F63**): kleptomania, pyromania, trichotillomania, intermittent explosive disorder (not in **ICD-10** but in **DSM-IV**) and pathological gambling. They are recurrent behaviours that appear irrational and harm the patient's own and others' interests; habitual excessive use of alcohol or drugs and sexual or eating-related compulsive acts are excluded. A repeated failure to resist impulses (to set fire, steal, pull one's own hair) is the common theme.

**ICD-10** recognises three gender identity disorders: transsexualism, dual role transvestism and gender identity disorder of childhood. Gender identity is established by 3 years, is the individual's self-perception of being male or female, depends on reared sex more than biological sex, and resists change once firmly established.

Gender dysphoria = feeling of incongruence between one's gender identity and phenotypic appearance, in various degrees. Dual role transvestism is a mild form: wearing clothes of the opposite sex to experience temporary membership of the opposite sex, with no sexual motivation and no desire for permanent change. It must be differentiated from fetishistic transvestism, where cross-dressing causes sexual arousal (a paraphilia).

blocks.title: Transsexualism criteria
rows: Persistent discomfort with his/her sex or sense of inappropriateness in the gender role of that sex
Strong, persistent cross-gender identification (not merely a desire for cultural advantages of the other sex); may come with wish to make the body congruent through surgery and hormones
Not concurrent with a physical intersex condition and not due to other functional psychiatric disorders
Causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas
Transsexual identity present persistently for at least two years

blocks.text: A man who wants an operation to look like a woman has **TRANSSEXUALISM**: in transvestism cross-dressing is episodic and occurs **WITHOUT** a desire for surgery or other extreme measures, and fetishistic transvestites experience sexual arousal - so dual-role and fetishistic transvestism are the distractors.

Most adult transsexuals have origins of symptoms in childhood. Gender identity disorders of childhood can also be present in adolescents; a 6-month duration criterion applies to the pre-pubertal group. Chromosomal and endocrine problems must be ruled out. In children, management centres on promoting tolerance of uncertainty and resisting pressure for quick solutions; surgery is not justified until adulthood.

A transsexual person need not be homosexual: gender identity must be differentiated from sexual orientation. In gender dysphoria of childhood, 1/3 to 2/3 of boys later appear homosexually oriented but very few persist as adult transsexuals. Gender identity disorders at any age are more common in males. Cross-dressing can be transient in stressful times, and mild gender dysphoria may intensify in depressive episodes.

Persistent preoccupation with castration or penectomy without a desire to acquire the characteristics of the other sex may be classed as gender identity disorder **not otherwise specified** or body dysmorphophobia, but is not transsexualism.

Paraphilias (disorders of sexual preference) are coded under **F60** in the source notes (p49). Reviewer correction (not in the source): ICD-10 codes paraphilias (disorders of sexual preference) at **F65**; F60 is specific personality disorders, F63 habit and impulse disorders and F64 gender identity disorders. The notes themselves write sexual compulsive acts as F65.- on p48. They involve ego-syntonic urges of sexual deviancy (except some exhibitionism where urges are reported as ego-alien).

blocks.text: Hyperkinetic disorder is the **attention deficit hyperactivity disorder** equivalent in **ICD-10**. The diagnostic criteria for **attention deficit hyperactivity disorder**/**hyperkinetic disorder** are considered more 'relaxed' in **DSM** but stricter in **ICD-10**.

**DSM-IV** **attention deficit hyperactivity disorder**: some symptoms must be present before age 7 (although often diagnosed later); impairment from inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity must be observable in at least 2 settings, interfere with developmentally appropriate functioning and persist for at least six months. **Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder** is not diagnosed when symptoms occur with a pervasive developmental disorder, schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder.

**DSM-5** **attention deficit hyperactivity disorder**: core symptoms must have onset **BEFORE** 12 years of age (**DSM-IV**: some symptoms before age 7); **DSM-5** also requires several symptoms in more than one setting and only 5 symptoms (not the usual 6) for individuals aged 17 or older.

blocks.text: Conduct disorder is an enduring set of antisocial and aggressive behaviours, usually aggression and violation of others' rights. Four categories: physical aggression or threats and cruelty to people and animals; destruction of own or others' property; theft or deceit; frequent serious violation of age-appropriate rules (truanting, running away).

Other features of conduct disorder: early sexual behaviour, lack of empathy, low self-esteem, gang involvement. Features usually present for at least six months. **DSM-IV**: the source notes (p56) print that behaviours begin before age 13 (childhood-onset type: symptoms before age 10; adolescent-onset type: after age 10). Reviewer correction (not in the source): the DSM-IV subtypes are childhood-onset type (at least one criterion present before age 10) and adolescent-onset type (no criterion before age 10); 'before age 13' applies only to specific criteria (staying out at night despite parental prohibition, and truanting from school), not to the onset of the disorder.

Oppositional defiant disorder: enduring negative, hostile, disobedient and defiant behaviour without serious violation of societal norms or others' rights; persistent for at least 6 months; temper outbursts, refusal to comply, blaming others, spiteful behaviour exceeding expectations for age. **ICD-10** regards it as a subtype (limited form) of conduct disorder; **DSM-IV** excludes oppositional disorder if conduct disorder is present.

DSM-5 adds disruptive mood dysregulation disorder: persistent irritability with outbursts 3 or more times a week for more than a year.
